paragraphs: Hybrid dynamical systems combine continuous motion with switches between discrete modes. Discovering their governing equations therefore involves two connected questions: which mode is active at each point, and which equation describes that mode? The paper argues that separating these questions can discard information needed to answer both well.

Earlier approaches first divide time series into small groups and then fit equations independently within those fragments. AMORE instead learns mode assignments and equations together in an end-to-end framework. Segments assigned to the same mode collectively inform its equation, allowing repeated appearances of the same dynamics to contribute to one shared description.

This matters because a fragment’s equation can help determine its mode, while its mode determines which other fragments provide relevant evidence. Joint learning preserves that relationship. Across four hybrid systems and six non-hybrid systems, the authors report better equation discovery, segmentation, and forecasting than previous methods. These results support sharing information across segments while jointly identifying the system’s modes.
icml-2024-amortized-equation-discovery-i.tldr: AMORE jointly identifies dynamical modes and their equations, pooling evidence across segments to improve discovery, segmentation, and forecasting in experiments.

paragraphs: Causal discovery often uses conditional independence tests to investigate whether observed relationships could reflect causal connections. Hidden variables can distort these tests, particularly when an unobserved factor influences multiple measured variables. Proxy variables provide indirect information about what is hidden, but previous proxy-based approaches restricted the variable types or imposed strong assumptions about functional form.

This paper introduces a hypothesis test for causal relationships between continuous variables without parametric constraints. Its central step is discretization: converting continuous observations into a form that supports a linear equation. Under completeness conditions, this equation emerges asymptotically, and its coefficient vector can be identified when the causal null hypothesis holds.

The authors build their test statistic around that identifiable structure and establish its asymptotic level and power, addressing false-positive control and detection ability as sample sizes grow. Synthetic and real-world evaluations support the procedure’s effectiveness. The contribution is a less parametrically restrictive route to proxy-assisted causal testing, while retaining the stated completeness conditions and asymptotic nature of its guarantees.
icml-2024-causal-discovery-via-condition.tldr: The paper develops a nonparametric proxy-based test for causal relationships among continuous variables, with asymptotic guarantees under completeness conditions.

paragraphs: When some node classes are much more common than others, graph classifiers can develop biased predictions. Common remedies change how often examples are sampled or how much each class contributes to training. This paper investigates another source of the problem: the graph’s connections can amplify the bias associated with unequal class frequencies.

The authors theoretically identify two topological phenomena that substantially worsen this bias. They use that analysis to design BAT, a lightweight framework that augments graph topology. Its intervention targets the structure through which graph learning operates, allowing it to reduce imbalance-related bias without changing class weights or resampling classes.

Because topology augmentation addresses a different part of the learning process, BAT can also be combined with existing class-rebalancing techniques. Experiments on real-world imbalanced graph tasks report gains of up to 46.27% in performance and reductions of up to 72.74% in bias over existing techniques. These are reported upper-end improvements, supporting topology as a useful complementary intervention rather than implying the same gain on every task.
icml-2024-class-imbalanced-graph-learnin.tldr: BAT reduces class-imbalance bias by augmenting graph topology and can also strengthen existing class-rebalancing methods.

paragraphs: Combinatorial bandit problems involve learning which combinations of uncertain choices produce good outcomes. This paper broadens that framework so each arm produces a multidimensional random outcome and feedback arrives through a general probabilistic triggering process. The resulting CMAB-MT framework can represent richer observations and interactions than formulations with simpler arm outcomes.

The authors introduce a smoothness condition that accounts for both multidimensional outcomes and arm-triggering probabilities. They then build an optimistic algorithm, CUCB-MT, around that condition. The approach uses distinct statistical properties of multivariant random variables to obtain improved results, making the richer representation useful for analysis as well as modeling.

Applications include episodic reinforcement learning and probabilistic maximum coverage for distributing goods. These problems satisfy the proposed condition and receive regret bounds matching or improving prior results. Regret measures the cost of learning through uncertain choices. By expressing episodic reinforcement learning through this bandit framework, the paper provides a connection that may enable further exchange of methods between the two research areas.
icml-2024-combinatorial-multivariant-mul.tldr: CMAB-MT models multidimensional bandit outcomes and probabilistic feedback, yielding matching or improved regret bounds for applications including episodic reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: High-dimensional functional time series involve many evolving functions, making forecasting a problem of both representing complex observations and modeling change over time. The Deep Functional Factor Model, or DF2M, addresses this through a Bayesian nonparametric factor model. Its structure is intended to make neural-network-based forecasting more explainable.

DF2M combines an Indian Buffet Process with a multi-task Gaussian Process and places a deep neural network inside the kernel function. This kernel captures nonlinear temporal relationships and non-Markovian dynamics, allowing the temporal description to extend beyond dependence on only the immediately preceding state. The factor model provides an explicit organizing structure around those learned relationships.

The authors also develop a computationally efficient variational inference algorithm for fitting the model. On four real-world datasets, they report better explainability and predictive accuracy than conventional deep learning approaches to high-dimensional functional time series. The findings support a design in which neural networks enrich a structured statistical model, combining flexible temporal modeling with a factor-based account of the data.
icml-2024-deep-functional-factor-models-.tldr: DF2M combines Bayesian factor modeling and deep kernels to improve explainability and forecasting accuracy on four functional time-series datasets.

paragraphs: Choosing a network’s width and depth is a central part of scaling its architecture. Automated neural architecture search can help, but searching efficiently remains difficult. Differentiable Model Scaling, or DMS, represents both choices in a directly differentiable form so that the architecture’s dimensions become easier to optimize.

The approach is evaluated across vision and language tasks, including convolutional networks and Transformers. This breadth matters because width and depth decisions occur in different architectures and applications. The reported results consistently favor the structures found by DMS over the compared architecture-search methods, supporting its usefulness across the tested settings.

On ImageNet, the authors report top-1 accuracy improvements of 1.4% for EfficientNet-B0 and 0.6% for Deit-Tiny, and a 1.3% advantage over ZiCo with 0.4 GPU days of searching. They also report a 2.0% mAP improvement for Yolo-v8-n on COCO. For language modeling, their pruned Llama-7B achieves lower perplexity and higher zero-shot classification accuracy than the prior method. Together, these findings connect efficient architecture search with improved task performance.
icml-2024-differentiable-model-scaling-u.tldr: DMS makes network width and depth differentiable search variables, finding improved architectures efficiently across tested vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: Semiparametric theory can produce statistically strong estimation procedures for problems such as missing data, causal inference, and transfer learning. Making those procedures practical can require solving Fredholm integral equations of the second kind. Traditional polynomial or spline approximations become difficult to scale when the problem involves multiple dimensions.

A computational shortcut is to replace the original equation with an easier one that has a closed-form solution. The paper explains that this can sacrifice statistical quality or even produce an incorrect procedure. DNA-SE instead formulates semiparametric estimation as a bi-level optimization problem and uses deep neural networks as numerical solvers within that framework.

The method draws on neural networks’ universal approximation property to support a scalable algorithm for these integral-equation problems. Numerical experiments and a real-data analysis show numerical and statistical advantages over traditional methods. The contribution places neural networks inside the computational machinery of semiparametric estimation, aiming to make its theoretically motivated procedures more practical without relying on the same equation-simplification shortcuts.
icml-2024-dna-se-towards-deep-neural-net.tldr: DNA-SE uses neural networks to solve integral equations within semiparametric estimation, showing computational and statistical advantages in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, reduces the number of parameters trained when adapting a pretrained model and avoids additional inference costs. Its accuracy nevertheless often trails full fine-tuning. This paper examines that gap by analyzing how weight changes differ between LoRA and full fine-tuning through a decomposition of the weights.

The resulting method, DoRA, separates a pretrained weight into magnitude and direction components for adaptation. It applies LoRA specifically to directional updates, keeping the number of trainable parameters small. This design aims to bring the learning capacity of the efficient adaptation method closer to that of full fine-tuning.

The authors report improvements in LoRA’s learning capacity and training stability without extra inference overhead. DoRA consistently outperforms LoRA in their fine-tuning experiments with LLaMA, LLaVA, and VL-BART, covering commonsense reasoning, visual instruction tuning, and image/video-text understanding. These findings support weight decomposition as a useful design choice for efficient adaptation; the stated comparison establishes gains over LoRA without claiming that DoRA universally matches full fine-tuning.
icml-2024-dora-weight-decomposed-low-ran.tldr: DoRA adapts weight magnitude and direction separately, improving on LoRA in reported experiments without additional inference overhead.

paragraphs: A language model can assign high likelihood to molecular token sequences without reliably producing valid molecules with desirable properties. A single incorrect token can invalidate a candidate, while generation shaped by prior training can balance exploration and exploitation poorly. The paper addresses this gap between token prediction and useful molecular generation.

Entropy-Reinforced Planning, or ERP, adds a planning algorithm to Transformer decoding. Its purpose is to balance exploiting promising choices with exploring alternatives, improving multiple molecular properties relative to direct Transformer sampling. The intervention focuses on how the model generates a sequence, using planning to guide that process.

The authors evaluate ERP on benchmarks involving the SARS-CoV-2 target 3CLPro and the human cancer cell target RTCB. They report improvements of 1–5% over the current state-of-the-art algorithm and 5–10% over baselines, with benefits persisting across Transformers trained using different objectives. ERP also outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approach on three code-generation benchmarks. These results suggest that its decoding strategy can help beyond the molecular tasks that motivated it.
icml-2024-entropy-reinforced-planning-wi.tldr: ERP guides Transformer decoding with entropy-reinforced planning, improving reported molecular-generation and code-generation benchmark results.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input differs from the data a model was trained to handle. Feature-based detectors can be effective, but building auxiliary models from training features adds computational overhead. This paper proposes using distances from an input’s features to the classifier’s decision boundaries without an auxiliary model.

To make this practical, the authors derive a closed-form estimate and prove that it tightly lower-bounds the distance. Using that estimate, they observe that in-distribution features tend to lie farther from decision boundaries than out-of-distribution features. They also find clearer separation when comparing samples with equal deviations from the mean training feature.

The detector therefore adjusts boundary distances according to that deviation, producing a method that requires neither hyperparameters nor an auxiliary model. Extensive experiments show effectiveness matching or exceeding state-of-the-art methods while adding negligible inference latency. The findings indicate that boundary geometry, interpreted alongside distance from the feature mean, can provide a useful detection signal at low computational cost.
icml-2024-fast-decision-boundary-based-o.tldr: The detector uses efficiently estimated feature-to-boundary distances to detect unfamiliar inputs with strong reported accuracy and negligible inference overhead.

paragraphs: Federated representation learning lets clients collaborate on a shared representation while keeping personalized prediction heads. This paper studies the under-parameterized case: the shared model lacks enough expressive capacity to capture all variation among the ground-truth client models. That makes choosing what information the common representation should retain especially important.

The proposed algorithm, FLUTE, starts from a data-independent random initialization and uses a carefully designed objective. The objective helps recover the subspace of the globally optimal representation from local representations that do not align. The analysis connects this federated learning problem with low-rank matrix approximation, providing a mathematical route to understanding the shared structure.

For linear models in this regime, the authors characterize FLUTE’s sample complexity and convergence rate, presenting it as the first such algorithm with provable performance guarantees to their knowledge. They also extend FLUTE beyond linear representations. Experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks show improvements over state-of-the-art federated representation learning methods, while the stated theoretical guarantees specifically concern the linear setting.
icml-2024-federated-representation-learn.tldr: FLUTE learns shared federated representations under limited model capacity, with guarantees for linear models and favorable synthetic and real-world results.

paragraphs: Protein motif scaffolding aims to build a surrounding structure that incorporates motifs associated with desired functions. Designing around several motifs is challenging because their relative positions may be unknown. The paper identifies fixed motif placement as a restriction of earlier approaches and notes that conditional generation does not guarantee motif inclusion.

Floating Anchor Diffusion, or FADiff, lets each motif move rigidly and independently during diffusion. Rigid motion preserves the motif’s internal structure while allowing its placement relative to other motifs to change. This mechanism guarantees that the motifs remain present and makes their positions part of the design process.

The authors report high success rates and novel scaffolds that are designable in their experiments. They describe FADiff as, to their knowledge, the first method to scaffold multiple motifs without requiring expert knowledge of their relative positions. The significance is that scaffold generation can jointly accommodate multiple prescribed motifs and determine their arrangement, addressing a structural design challenge relevant to constructing proteins with multiple desired functions.
icml-2024-floating-anchor-diffusion-mode.tldr: FADiff designs scaffolds around multiple preserved protein motifs while automatically determining their relative positions.

paragraphs: A marginal probability describes part of a data configuration while leaving the remaining variables unspecified. Computing arbitrary marginals efficiently is difficult for high-dimensional discrete generative models. Marginalization models, or MAMs, address this by explicitly modeling the family of marginal distributions induced by the full distribution.

A MAM approximates an arbitrary marginal probability with a single neural-network forward pass. The authors develop scalable learning methods based on marginalization self-consistency, so the learned marginals are trained around their mutual relationships. They also tackle energy-based training, where the target distribution is specified through an unnormalized log-probability function such as an energy or reward.

Evaluations cover images, text, physical systems, and molecules under both maximum-likelihood and energy-based training. The authors report orders-of-magnitude faster marginal-probability evaluation in both settings. For energy-based training, they also demonstrate any-order generative modeling at higher dimensional scales than previous methods. The contribution combines faster access to partial probabilities with a training approach that supports larger discrete generative problems.
icml-2024-generative-marginalization-mod.tldr: MAMs approximate arbitrary discrete marginal probabilities in one forward pass, delivering large reported speedups and more scalable energy-based generative modeling.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization protects against distribution shifts by minimizing risk under the worst distribution within an uncertainty set. That caution can become excessive, producing low-confidence predictions, poor parameter estimates, and weak generalization. This paper investigates excessive attention to noisy samples as a probable cause of that over-pessimism.

The proposed Geometry-Calibrated DRO, or GCDRO, incorporates the geometry of the data into calibration terms for regression. These terms are designed to reduce the impact of noise. The authors connect the resulting risk objective to Helmholtz free energy from statistical physics and show that this free-energy-based risk perspective can extend to standard DRO methods.

They also develop an approximate minimax optimization algorithm using gradient flow in Wasserstein space, with a bounded error ratio. The analysis explains how the approach mitigates noisy-sample effects, while comprehensive experiments report superiority over conventional DRO methods. Together, the results support using data geometry to calibrate robustness so that noisy observations exert less influence on the worst-case optimization.
icml-2024-geometry-calibrated-dro-combat.tldr: GCDRO uses data geometry to reduce noise-driven over-pessimism in robust regression, with theoretical analysis and favorable experimental comparisons.

paragraphs: Optimizing a non-smooth, non-convex objective is difficult when stochastic gradients can have large, heavy-tailed fluctuations. Earlier online-to-non-convex results assumed bounded gradient variance and provided guarantees in expectation. This paper seeks a stationary point with high probability under the weaker requirement of a finite p-th gradient moment, for p between one and two.

The algorithm first adds gradient clipping to the online-to-non-convex framework, limiting extreme gradient contributions while generating candidate points. It then uses a validation procedure to select a candidate meeting the required stationarity criterion. This second step turns a guarantee about the generated sequence into a high-probability statement about a selected output.

The resulting gradient complexity is approximately epsilon raised to minus (2p−1)/(p−1), multiplied by delta inverse, with logarithmic factors suppressed. When p equals two, the bound becomes approximately epsilon to minus three times delta inverse, improving the prior high-probability epsilon-to-minus-four dependence. The authors also establish a separate bound for smooth objectives. These guarantees concern approximate stationarity under the stated moment conditions.
icml-2024-high-probability-bound-for-non.tldr: Gradient clipping and candidate validation yield improved high-probability stationarity guarantees for stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed gradients.

paragraphs: Useful communication does not always involve giving every detail with maximum precision. People may round a time or omit information to help a listener make a decision. This paper investigates how language models handle these nuanced tensions between honesty and helpfulness, using psychological models and experiments originally designed to characterize human behavior.

The researchers test multiple language models and examine two ways their responses can change: optimization for human preferences and reasoning during inference. In the studied settings, reinforcement learning from human feedback improves both honesty and helpfulness. Chain-of-thought prompting instead shifts responses toward helpfulness relative to honesty, showing that these interventions affect the balance differently.

GPT-4 Turbo also displays human-like response patterns, including sensitivity to conversational framing and the listener’s decision context. These findings describe observable communication choices in the experiments. They suggest that models internalize patterns associated with conversational values and that zero-shot prompts can steer even these abstract priorities to some degree, without establishing unrestricted control over honesty or helpfulness.
icml-2024-how-do-large-language-models-n.tldr: Psychology-based experiments show that preference training and reasoning prompts affect how language models balance honesty and helpfulness.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph reasoning uses relationships among entities to infer further connections. Path-based methods have performed well, but their message-passing machinery can miss useful paths or compress too much information into limited representations. KnowFormer revisits Transformers as a way to address these constraints through reasoning over graph structure.

The model defines attention around the query structure of knowledge graph reasoning. It introduces structure-aware modules for computing queries, keys, and values, allowing self-attention to incorporate information about the graph. This makes its use of a Transformer distinct from approaches that rely on pretrained language models to reason through textual information.

The authors also provide an efficient attention computation method to improve scalability. Experiments show that KnowFormer outperforms prominent baselines on both transductive and inductive benchmarks, covering both evaluation settings reported in the paper. The results support adapting attention specifically to graph reasoning queries and structure, while the efficient computation addresses the practical cost of applying that mechanism at greater scale.
icml-2024-knowformer-revisiting-transfor.tldr: KnowFormer uses efficient, structure-aware Transformer attention for knowledge graph reasoning and outperforms prominent baselines on the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Multi-label image recognition asks a model to identify several applicable labels in one image. Adapting vision-language models for this task often requires images annotated with multiple labels, which are difficult to obtain at scale. This paper proposes training the task classifier from language data without requiring annotated images.

The method uses language generated by large language models together with CLIP’s aligned image and text embedding space. A classifier trained in the language modality is then transferred to visual inputs. This approach makes the shared embedding space the connection between the training information supplied as text and the images classified at inference.

Direct transfer can lose performance because image and language embeddings still differ. The authors therefore introduce a mapping that moves image embeddings toward the language modality while retaining crucial visual information. Experiments show improvements over other zero-shot multi-label recognition methods and competitive performance against few-shot methods. These findings support combining language-driven classifier training with an explicit correction for the modality gap.
icml-2024-language-driven-cross-modal-cl.tldr: The framework trains a multi-label image classifier from generated language and maps image embeddings into the language modality for effective transfer.

paragraphs: Language models can generate harmful content biased against demographic groups. Previous debiasing methods intervene by removing attitude or demographic information, but this can reduce generation quality. The paper asks how much fluency must actually be sacrificed to achieve a desired fairness level, treating the trade-off as a formal information-theoretic problem.

The authors’ analysis finds that previous approaches intervene more extensively than needed for debiasing. They propose LIDAO, a general framework with a provable improvement in fluency for the debiasing problem they study. Its central motivation is to limit the intervention while still addressing the targeted fairness issue.

The framework is also strengthened for adversarial prompts that induce unfairness visible only when the generated response is interpreted together with the prompt. This expands the treatment from generated text alone to its conversational context. Experiments on three language models ranging from 0.7 billion to 7 billion parameters show the method’s superiority in the reported evaluations. The contribution combines a formal treatment of the fairness–fluency trade-off with context-sensitive debiasing.
icml-2024-lidao-towards-limited-interven.tldr: LIDAO uses limited, theoretically motivated interventions to improve the fairness–fluency trade-off and address unfairness arising from prompt–response context.

paragraphs: Sample average approximation solves a stochastic optimization problem by replacing an expected objective with an average over sampled observations. A central theoretical question is how many samples are needed for a useful solution. This paper studies that question for convex and strongly convex problems, including a simple regularized version of the method.

The analysis works under heavy-tailed assumptions and regularity conditions comparable to those in typical sample-average-approximation research. Its main result removes any complexity measure of the feasible region from the sample-complexity bounds. Such measures include the logarithm of a covering number, which describes how extensively the allowable solution set must be represented at a chosen resolution.

Removing that dependence changes what drives the theoretical sample requirement. The resulting bounds can have more favorable dependence on problem dimensionality than state-of-the-art bounds. This is a conditional advantage under the paper’s assumptions, rather than a claim that every high-dimensional problem needs fewer samples. The contribution is a sharper theoretical assessment of familiar approximation procedures, including their regularized variation.
icml-2024-new-sample-complexity-bounds-f.tldr: The paper derives heavy-tailed sample-average-approximation bounds free of feasible-region complexity measures, potentially improving dependence on dimensionality.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning trains node representations by bringing positive pairs together and separating negative pairs. This paper asks how graph augmentations shape the usefulness of those representations for downstream tasks. It investigates why augmentation choice and strength matter, and whether stronger alignment necessarily leads to better task performance.

The analysis finds that the main downstream contribution comes from separating different classes, rather than collecting all members of a class into the same representation. It further finds that making positive pairs perfectly identical can improve the contrastive objective while harming generalization. A better training loss therefore may not correspond to the best downstream accuracy.

The authors examine these results through information theory and graph spectrum theory, then propose two simple methods to test their ideas. The methods can be applied to various graph contrastive learning algorithms, and extensive experiments support their effectiveness. The practical implication is to design augmentations that achieve an appropriate degree of alignment, using downstream generalization as a guide rather than treating perfect alignment as the goal.
icml-2024-perfect-alignment-may-be-poiso.tldr: The paper finds that perfect positive-pair alignment can hurt graph contrastive learning’s generalization and motivates augmentations that balance alignment appropriately.

paragraphs: This paper studies reconstructing a symmetric, positive semidefinite, low-rank matrix when observed entries depend deterministically on their values. Under ReLU sampling, only positive entries are visible; a broader version uses thresholds. Because visibility depends on the unknown entries themselves, the sampling rule is central to the reconstruction problem.

The authors empirically show that gradient descent from random initialization generally reaches stationary points that are not globally optimal. They nevertheless prove a favorable local property: under mild assumptions on a small-rank matrix factor, the objective has geodesic strong convexity near the planted matrix on a quotient manifold. They also show that factors with independent Gaussian entries satisfy their assumptions.

Building on this local structure, the paper develops a tailored initialization for gradient descent. In the reported experiments, it always converges to global minima. Additional experiments examine initialization, noise, dimension, and rank. The key distinction is between the proved local geometry and the observed global-minimum convergence of the initialized algorithm; the empirical outcome does not turn the entire optimization landscape into a globally benign one.
icml-2024-symmetric-matrix-completion-wi.tldr: For matrix completion from positive entries, the paper proves favorable local geometry and designs an initialization that reaches global minima in its experiments.

paragraphs: Explaining a time-series model requires identifying meaningful information in its input signals. This paper examines explanation learning through information theory and finds that many existing explainability measures may admit trivial solutions or create distribution shifts. An explanation can therefore score well under a measure while failing to provide the intended kind of insight.

The authors introduce a modified information-bottleneck objective designed to avoid those problems. They build TimeX++ around it, using a parametric network to generate instances with explanations embedded in them. These generated instances are designed to remain within the data distribution and preserve the label, keeping the explanation connected to the original prediction task.

The framework is evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively on synthetic and real-world datasets, with additional case studies in an environmental application. TimeX++ outperforms the compared leading baselines across all evaluated datasets. These findings support treating distributional validity and label preservation as integral parts of explanation learning, alongside the information-based objective used to identify useful explanatory content.
icml-2024-timex-learning-time-series-exp.tldr: TimeX++ learns time-series explanations with a modified information-bottleneck objective that targets trivial solutions and distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Generative models serve three closely related purposes: creating new examples, reconstructing existing inputs, and learning compact representations. Different model families tend to favor particular capabilities or data types. This paper introduces Encoding-Decoding Diffusion Probabilistic Models, or EDDPMs, to combine these capabilities in a framework applicable to both discrete and continuous data.

EDDPMs generalize the Gaussian noising and denoising process of standard diffusion by introducing parameterized encoding and decoding. The encoder and decoder are learned jointly with diffusion while remaining compatible with established diffusion objectives and training recipes. This makes the representation-producing components part of the same learning process as generation.

Appropriate encoder and decoder choices, including large language models, let the framework accommodate different kinds of inputs. Experiments on text, proteins, and images demonstrate flexibility across data types and tasks, together with strong improvements over the compared models. The findings support jointly adapting encoding, decoding, and diffusion as a way to bring generation, reconstruction, and representation learning into one model family.
icml-2024-unified-generation-reconstruct.tldr: EDDPMs jointly learn encoding, decoding, and diffusion to support generation, reconstruction, and representation learning across text, proteins, and images.

paragraphs: Self-supervised ECG learning can extract representations from unannotated recordings, but it often overlooks clinical information in associated reports and still requires labeled examples for downstream tasks. MERL addresses both issues by learning jointly from ECG records and their reports, enabling classification through text prompts without downstream training data.

At test time, the authors add Clinical Knowledge Enhanced Prompt Engineering, or CKEPE. It uses large language models with external, expert-verified clinical knowledge databases to produce more descriptive prompts. The approach is intended to reduce hallucinations in generated content and strengthen the text descriptions used for zero-shot ECG classification.

Across six public ECG datasets, MERL achieves an average zero-shot AUC of 75.2%. The authors report this as 3.2% higher than linear-probed self-supervised ECG methods using 10% annotated training data. The absence of training data refers to the downstream classification tasks; MERL itself learns from paired records and reports. These results support combining multimodal pretraining with clinically informed test-time prompts to reduce downstream annotation requirements.
icml-2024-zero-shot-ecg-classification-w.tldr: MERL learns from ECG–report pairs and uses clinically enhanced text prompts to classify ECGs without downstream training data.
